body:
Madhavpur Ghed Fair

The Madhavpur Ghed Fair is held at Madhavpur Ghed, a coastal village in Porbandar district. It is associated with the Madhavrai Temple and the traditional account of the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.

Time of celebration

The annual fair begins on Ram Navami, which falls on Chaitra Sud 9. The traditional festivities continue until Chaitra Sud 13, generally during March or April.

Religious and cultural significance

According to local folklore, Madhavpur was the place where Krishna married Rukmini, the daughter of King Bhishmaka. The fair commemorates this marriage through religious ceremonies, cultural programmes and traditional celebrations.

The religious association should be distinguished from the date of commencement. Although the fair begins on Ram Navami, it commemorates the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.

Connection with northeastern India

The Madhavpur Ghed Fair has a distinctive association with the cultural traditions of northeastern India. The Mishmi community of Arunachal Pradesh traditionally traces its ancestry to King Bhishmaka.

Since 2018, the Government of Gujarat and the Union Ministry of Culture have collaborated in organising the fair on an expanded cultural scale. It promotes interaction between Gujarat and the northeastern states through folk arts, handicrafts, music and other cultural traditions.

This cultural connection reflects the objective of Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat, which promotes mutual understanding among different regions of India.

Madhavpur Ghed belongs to Porbandar district. Its calendar association is Ram Navami, while its principal religious association is the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.

Rann Utsav

Rann Utsav is a seasonal cultural and tourism festival held at Dhordo village in Kutch district, near the White Rann of the Great Rann of Kutch.

Unlike most traditional fairs that centre on a particular lunar date, Rann Utsav is organised as an extended winter festival.

Time and development

The festival generally takes place during the winter tourism season, approximately from November to February or March. The precise opening and closing dates vary between editions.

Rann Utsav was introduced in 2005 by the Tourism Corporation of Gujarat Limited. It developed from a short celebration into an extended tourism festival showcasing the natural landscape and cultural heritage of Kutch.

For the 2026-27 edition, Gujarat Tourism lists the scheduled period of Rann Utsav Tent City as 1 November 2026 to 7 March 2027. As of 26 November 2026, this is the announced schedule for the edition, rather than a permanent annual date.

Communities and cultural features

The festival showcases the traditions of Kutchi communities, including local artisans, craftspeople and folk performers. It provides opportunities to exhibit and sell regional handicrafts such as embroidery, Bandhani, Ajrakh printing and other traditional products.

Dhordo is located in the Banni region and is associated with traditional Mutwa embroidery. However, Rann Utsav represents the wider cultural diversity of Kutch and is not restricted to a single community.

The White Rann, traditional music and dance, regional cuisine, craft exhibitions and tented accommodation are important features of the festival.

Comparison of the 2 cultural gatherings

AttributeMadhavpur GhedRann Utsav
DistrictPorbandarKutch
SettingCoastal village and templeWhite salt desert
TimeChaitra, March-AprilExtended winter season
Central themeMarriage of Krishna and RukminiKutchi heritage and tourism
Community connectionGujarat and northeastern IndiaKutchi artisan communities

Prelims focus

  • Madhavpur Ghed Fair is held in Porbandar district.
  • It begins on Ram Navami and commemorates the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.
  • The Mishmi community of Arunachal Pradesh is associated with its northeastern cultural connection.
  • Rann Utsav is centred at Dhordo in Kutch district.
  • Rann Utsav was introduced in 2005 and is an extended winter tourism festival.
  • Trap: Rann Utsav does not have a single fixed annual lunar date.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, printed p. 4; Press Information Bureau, President of India Inaugurates Madhavpur Ghed Fair, 10 April 2022; Press Information Bureau, Madhavpur Mela and Northeastern Cultural Integration, release dated 2020, PRID 1598796; Gujarat Tourism, Madhavpur Fair and Rann Utsav, History, When, Where and Interesting Facts. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

Fair, place, district and traditional timing

The following table brings together the 10 important fairs and cultural gatherings of Gujarat. Their traditional occasions provide a more reliable basis for identification than individual years' Gregorian calendar dates.

FairPlaceDistrictTraditional timing

VauthaVautha, DholkaAhmedabadKartik Purnima; usually November
ShamlajiShamlaji, Shamlaji talukaAravalliKartik Sud 11 to Purnima; usually November
BhavnathGirnar TaletiJunagadhMaha Vad, Mahashivratri; February-March
Dang DarbarAhwaDangFagan, before and around Holi; usually March
KavantKavant or KwantChhota UdepurUsually 3rd day after Holi
Gol GadhedaJesawada, GarbadaDahodAfter Holi, commonly 5-7 days later; local variation exists
Chitra-VichitraGunbhakhari near KhedbrahmaSabarkanthaAbout 2 weeks after Holi, near Amavasya; March-April
Madhavpur GhedMadhavpurPorbandarChaitra Sud 9-13; March-April
Rann UtsavDhordoKutchWinter season; approximately November-March

Fair, community and distinctive feature

FairPrincipal community associationIdentifying feature
TarnetarKolis, Rabaris, Bharwads and other Saurashtra communitiesEmbroidered umbrellas and matchmaking
VauthaPastoral groups, animal traders and pilgrimsDonkey trading and Saptasangam
ShamlajiBhils and other devoteesVishnu pilgrimage and Meshwo River
BhavnathNaga sadhus, pilgrims, Ahirs and MersMahashivratri and Mrigi Kund
Dang DarbarBhils, Kunbis, Warlis and GamitsTraditional tribal rulers and chiefs
KavantRathwaHarvest and tribal celebration
Gol GadhedaTribal communities of the Dahod region, particularly the Bhil cultural regionJaggery-pole competition
Chitra-VichitraBhil and GarasiaMourning deceased relatives and matchmaking
Madhavpur GhedGujarati and northeastern communities, including the Mishmi cultural connectionMarriage of Krishna and Rukmini
Rann UtsavKutchi artisans and folk performersWhite Rann and winter cultural tourism

These community associations identify important traditions and participants. They do not imply that attendance is restricted to those communities.

Important distinctions between similar fairs

Fairs at sacred river confluences

Vautha and Chitra-Vichitra are both associated with sacred river confluences. Vautha is identified with Saptasangam and Kartik Purnima. Chitra-Vichitra is identified with Triveni Sangam and the post-Holi new moon.

Fairs associated with donkeys

Vautha is a livestock trading fair famous for donkeys. Gol Gadheda derives its name from a customary competition involving jaggery and is not primarily a livestock market.

Fairs associated with marriage traditions

Tarnetar is associated with the legend of Draupadi's swayamvara and traditional matchmaking. Gol Gadheda preserves a competition historically connected with selecting marriage partners. Chitra-Vichitra provides opportunities for social gatherings and matchmaking. Madhavpur Ghed, in contrast, commemorates the legendary marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.

Districts in northern and eastern Gujarat

Shamlaji belongs to Aravalli district, whereas Gunbhakhari, the site of Chitra-Vichitra, belongs to Sabarkantha district. Kavant belongs to Chhota Udepur, while Jesawada, the site of Gol Gadheda, belongs to Dahod.

Fairs before and after Holi

Dang Darbar generally precedes Holi. Kavant, Gol Gadheda and Chitra-Vichitra follow Holi, with Chitra-Vichitra occurring near the next new moon. Madhavpur Ghed follows during Chaitra and begins on Ram Navami.

Prelims focus

  • Kartik Purnima: Vautha and Shamlaji.
  • Mahashivratri: Bhavnath, Junagadh.
  • Before Holi: Dang Darbar, Ahwa.
  • After Holi: Kavant, Gol Gadheda and Chitra-Vichitra.
  • Ram Navami: Madhavpur Ghed, Porbandar.
  • Extended winter season: Rann Utsav, Dhordo.

Annual sequence of the principal gatherings

The Gujarati annual calendar begins with Kartak after Diwali. Vautha and Shamlaji belong to this early part of the Gujarati year. The winter season includes Rann Utsav and is followed by the Mahashivratri and Holi-related fairs. Madhavpur Ghed follows in Chaitra, while Tarnetar occurs later in the year during Bhadarvo.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 1, Heritage of India, printed p. 4; Gujarat Tourism, individual fair and festival entries for Tarnetar, Mahashivratri Mela, Dang Darbar, Kavant, Chitra Vichitra, Madhavpur and Rann Utsav; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Vautha Mela and Shamlaji Mela; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Gol Gadheda Fair; Aravalli and Dahod district administration websites; Press Information Bureau, Madhavpur Ghed Fair, 10 April 2022. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
